newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe spruces up for OAU but blemishes remain.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe spruces up for OAU but blemishes remain.

text.p: Zimbabwe has been sprucing itself up for months for an Organisation of African Unity summit on June 2-4, but cannot hide the ugly spots on its political face.
Many Zimbabweans see their southern Africa country as a microcosm of the continent, full of economic potential but struggling to come to terms with daunting challenges.

"(OAU delegates) will find us in a raging debate on politics, democracy, abuse of office, corruption. They will find us debating the economy, unemployment, unfulfilled promises and public frustration," said political analyst Lupi Mushayakarara.
"Some of them will find themselves in us."

President Robert Mugabe's government, in power since 1980, is battling allegations of financial irregularities, which some analysts say may drown its members' proud legacy as "liberators of the majority black population from white minority rule".

Although the country -- blessed with a solid infrastructure and a working bureaucracy -- is not yet suffering the endemic corruption and bribery associated with some other parts of Africa, many say it is sliding towards generalised rot.
Week after week, the independent media has recently been reporting tales of alleged corruption and abuse of power. These have included:
--charges of favouritism in awarding multi-billion-dollar government tenders
--allegations that cabinet ministers and others raided a Z$450 million ($40 million) war victims' compensation fund in the last nine months.
--accusations that the rich and powerful abused a fund meant to house the homeless by building extra luxury homes for themselves.
--charges that government has done nothing in the last three years to recover land grabbed by government ministers under a programme meant to benefit the jobless, or land-hungry peasants.
The government, which accuses its opponents of running a smear campaign to discredit it, vehemently denies there is "wilful corruption" and says it is investigating all charges.
Mugabe's ruling ZANU-PF party has vowed to hit back with a campaign aimed at restoring the public focus to its early successes in expanding education and health services.
Its critics say, however, the current challenge is to deliver a transparent, accountable and democratic system.

"There is growing anger on the ground that the government is short-changing everybody except the top brass in almost every sphere," says John Makumbe, a political scientist at Harare's University of Zimbabwe.

But a weak and fractious political opposition has gained little mileage from the corruption charges, with quite a number of people ruling it out as a viable alternative government and preferring to keep "pressure to deliver" on ZANU-PF.
Political analysts say ZANU-PF -- like many other parties in Africa -- has perpetuated its dominance through a state-funded patronage system and allegedly biased electoral rules.
The ruling party still has a strong hold on the rural poor who still fondly remember its guerrilla war against Ian Smith's white minority rule that led to independence in 1980.
But there is urban discontent at the cost of living, whose sharp rise most people blame on alleged state mismanagement.
A bloated civil service and government spending that accounts for about 40 percent of gross domestic product are seen as a big drawback on industrial growth.
Zimbabwe's agriculture-based economy has grown at less than one percent annually in the last 10 years and has failed to curb rising unemployment, now estimated at up to 50 percent.

The government record on these issues is routinely denounced in the private media which is also pressing Mugabe to sack "arrogant leaders who dismiss public complaints with nauseating contempt", as one newspaper put it.
Mugabe is also wrestling with the dead.

On the eve of the OAU summit, the human rights group Amnesty International joined Zimbabwean civic organisations in appealing to him to acknowledge that his army murdered thousands of civilians during an anti-government rebellion in the 1980s.

"In this organisation's experience, when a state continues to deny its responsibility for atrocities committed by its security forces and suppresses open dialogue about human rights violations, a sense of impunity is created as the members of state agencies feel that they can abuse human rights without being punished," Amnesty said in a letter to Mugabe.
He becomes OAU chairman for a year at the summit.
